author: Amber Coakley
title: Venomous vipers, crocodile, other reptiles found hidden in car at San Diego border - NewsBreak
text:
By Amber Coakley ,
8 hours ago
SAN DIEGO (FOX 5/KUSI) — A woman accused of participating in a years-long exotic wildlife trafficking operation appeared in federal court Tuesday after authorities found dozens of reptiles hidden inside her car at the San Ysidro Port of Entry.
Georgina Bribiesca Chavez, a 66-year-old resident of Tijuana, Mexico, is facing a wildlife trafficking charge. Her alleged trafficking partner, 28-year-old Salvador Pelayo of Chula Vista, was arrested in July and faces a similar charge.
Authorities said Chavez was arrested last week while attempting to enter the United States in a red Volkswagen containing dozens of concealed reptiles, including four venomous yellow-blotched palm pit vipers, three caimans, a baby crocodile and more than 60 abronia lizards. An indigo snake was also found inside the vehicle.
According to court documents, Chavez arrived at the San Ysidro Port of Entry on Aug. 10 and told a U.S. Customs and Border Protection officer that she had nothing to declare. During an identification check, the officer discovered an outstanding arrest warrant connected to a long-term wildlife trafficking investigation.
Chavez was taken into custody and her vehicle was seized.
The next morning, CBP officers inspecting the Volkswagen discovered concealed factory compartments behind the rear bench seat. Inside were pillowcases that had been knotted shut and sealed with tape. One of the pillow cases was moving, according to court documents.

(U.S. Attorney's Office of Southern California) The packages were later taken to the San Diego Zoo, where staff carefully opened them and discovered the reptiles.
Authorities said several of the species are protected under international treaties because of declining populations.

(U.S. Attorney's Office of Southern California) The animals had reportedly been trapped inside the vehicle for nearly 24 hours during August heat in San Ysidro. All three caimans died before San Diego Zoo staff could provide care, while the remaining animals were reported to be stable and under the zoo's care as of last week.
“These animals were not cargo — they were living creatures subjected to dangerous conditions for profit,” said U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon.
Drug bust: $238K worth of fentanyl found in moped at San Diego border Alleged years-long trafficking operation Federal investigators say Chavez and Pelayo began working together in 2023 to traffic wildlife into the U.S. for sale to American buyers.
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service launched an undercover investigation about 18 months ago. Court documents allege the pair participated in undercover purchases involving protected turtles and were monitored while sending and receiving wildlife at shipping centers in San Diego County.
In March 2025, undercover agents allegedly purchased four protected Mexican box turtles from Pelayo and their partner in Mexico. Chavez allegedly met an undercover buyer at a Carlsbad outlet shopping center after crossing the border and delivered the live turtles in exchange for $2,600.
(U.S. Attorney's Office of Southern California) The turtles were transferred to the Oakland Zoo and identified as protected species native to Mexico. Court documents say all four were in poor health and likely had been caught in the wild and contracted respiratory disease. All four later died.
In another alleged transaction that month, an undercover agent purchased four protected Mexican and Yucatan box turtles that were shipped to New York.
Pelayo allegedly used the name “Jose Lopez” to mail the turtles to the undercover buyer on March 11, 2025. The animals were received the following day and transferred to the Buffalo Zoo.
Investigators also allege the pair exported wildlife from the U.S. to Mexico. Chavez was allegedly seen picking up Eastern box turtles native to New York at a San Diego shipping center before smuggling them into Mexico in the trunk of her Volkswagen.
Court documents allege Chavez and Pelayo made tens of thousands of dollars from selling rare and protected animals to buyers in the U.S. and Mexico.
Pelayo was arrested in July and has pleaded not guilty to the federal wildlife trafficking charge.
Authorities said a search of his Chula Vista home on July 21 allegedly uncovered a snake believed to be an albino California kingsnake.
Chavez and Pelayo have both pleaded not guilty.
At Tuesday's hearing, U.S. Magistrate Judge Jill L. Burkhardt ordered Chavez held without bond pending trial.
Chavez is scheduled to return to federal court Aug. 27, 2026, for a preliminary hearing. Pelayo's next hearing is scheduled for Oct. 2, 2026.
If found guilty, the pair could face up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.
